Every documented flag, env var, command example, or output format must be verified against actual, current behavior before it is published. If a discrepancy is found, fix the root cause rather than normalizing it in prose:

- If a feature is broken or disabled, fix the code (or remove the feature) so the docs can describe real behavior, instead of documenting that it "has no effect." A caveat note implies the feature will work again soon; if there's no concrete plan to fix it, delete the documentation entry rather than describing dead functionality.
- If an example command is wrong (e.g., `cline connect telegram --restart -k <BOT-TOKEN>` failing because of argument-parsing order, or `--retries` crashing with no value), fix the underlying CLI/tool so the example works as written, and add a test that locks in the corrected behavior. Don't just patch the doc to work around a bug.
- Reference tables (e.g., JSON output `type` values, CLI flags, config keys) should reflect what consumers actually need to act on. Avoid claiming a table is "exhaustive" unless it truly is; instead instruct readers to skip unrecognized values, and omit internal/status-only entries that require no action.
- Watch for environment- or build-specific divergence (e.g., nightly vs. stable settings keys, legacy vs. new extension bundles). Verify docs against each variant your users might hit, and prefer fixing the inconsistency in code so one doc description covers all cases.

When documenting unavoidable caveats or exceptions (e.g., "hooks don't run for providers that handle tool calls themselves"), give complete, user-actionable guidance — explain the general rule or class of cases, not just a partial list of examples — so readers aren't left guessing whether their specific case is covered.
